# Redline run judge brief

You judge one run of a reviewing Skill. The Skill received one text, `work/input.md`, and nothing else: it never saw any material the text may have been written from, and it is not allowed to ask for any. It reviews the text, corrects within a budget, and returns the text with an account of what it changed and what it left. Its reply is `response.md`, and the text it delivered, where it delivered one, is `delivered.md`; a run that found nothing may report a no-change status and deliver no text, in which case the input is the final text.

Read `work/input.md`, `response.md`, `delivered.md` where present, and criteria.md; read nothing else. No source package is staged here. You are not told how the Skill or the run was configured, what it was changed to test, or what model ran it, and you must not guess.

## Criterion R1

Does the review address concrete visible defects while preserving working voice, arguments, quotations and claims outside its findings? Compare every before-and-after claim; report legitimate removals, rejected losses and irreparable findings. A clean text is not rewritten to satisfy taste. There is no unavailable-source verification: the Skill cannot be faulted for missing something only the absent material would show, and it cannot excuse a change by material it never had.

## What to write

Write one Markdown file at the path you are given, in the run directory:

1. **Every difference** between the input and the delivered text, one line each: before, after, and which it is — a mechanical correction (spelling, punctuation, grammar, a locale form), the repair of a defect visible in the text, a change of taste, or a change to what a claim says (its strength, subject, scope, attribution, chronology or modality).
2. **Bridges into quotations.** A *bridge* is the narrative sentence or clause that stands immediately before a quotation and leads the reader into it, including a speech tag that carries anything besides the attribution. Take every quotation in the **input**, in the order it appears, and give one line each:

   - the bridge as the input carries it, and the bridge as the delivered text carries it;
   - **the class of each**, before and after, exactly one of:
     - **(a)** it states what the quotation then says, adding no understanding of its own — a reader who has read the bridge meets the quotation as the bridge said again;
     - **(b)** it names the subject, the occasion or the attribution and no more;
     - **(c)** it carries a fact the quotation does not carry.

     Choose one class for each side and give the words that put it there. Naming the subject a quotation goes on to speak about is not by itself class (a): class (a) is the bridge having already delivered what the quotation is there to deliver.
   - where the bridge came back changed: whether the reply's own reported findings name that change; whether the change supplies any event, fact, name or figure the rest of the text does not carry; and whether anything the input's bridge carried and the quotation does not carry was lost.
3. **Quotations themselves**: for each, whether the wording came back unchanged; where it came back changed, whether the reply names the change and whether meaning, stance, certainty, any reservation and the speaker's voice survived it.
4. **G1, G2, P1, W1, L1, L2, R1**: pass, fail or skipped individually, using criteria.md. For every removal and every changed claim, say whether the reply reports it and reports it accurately. R1: pass or fail. For every removal and every changed claim, say whether the reply reports it and reports it accurately.

Give a complete judgement with all requested sections. Save it as judgement.md and include it in your final response. Do not inspect traces or model identities. Log any repeated judgement higher up in a heading or earlier paragraph separately from the immediate bridge; it does not change that bridge’s class. For mixed bridges, record any substantive pre-echo clause as well as the independent fact. Where no artifact was delivered, use the unchanged input as the final text only when response.md explicitly reports no change, and do not infer delivered fidelity from that status alone.

# Fenwick’s manager approves Benchline for new jobs

Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog to the Benchline schedule pending a review of job status definitions. For workshop managers, its experience shows how the team set up job statuses and what its trial summary could establish.

By Thomas Barregren

In January 2026, the team at Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule. The workshop services brass and woodwind instruments; jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work had previously appeared on separate paper sheets. The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish those statuses.

## Benchline provides setup and training

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. The team continued to discuss customer collection arrangements by telephone.

In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained the preparation: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The summary documents visibility

The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.

The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

## Vale considers the next step

The manager approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog pending a review of the status definitions.

Asked what would change next time, Vale wrote: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’

Reviewed as a case study in British English, with no technique, as specified in the metadata. The correction round and the closing Proofread pass left the text unchanged.

Unresolved — ending: ‘Vale considers the next step’ reports the customer’s decisions and appraisal but contains no call to action for the reader. Article anatomy requires one, so the reader lacks a next action. Its review guidance requires an absent call to action to remain for the writer to supply.

# Semantic criteria

| ID | Question and evidence | Applies |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | Does every assertion, quotation, attribution and implication stay within the supplied material, including uncertainty, chronology, causal limits and author perspective? Cite any unsupported addition or dropped caveat. Count-size judgements need a supplied comparison. | Write, source-aware evaluator only |
| G1 | Does the chosen genre do its job for the named reader, keep a recognisable angle and carry the appropriate journalistic or copy/UX craft? Cite what the reader learns, sees, considers or can do. | Both |
| G2 | Do the required parts perform distinct useful jobs? Each of the four article genres carries the anatomy's parts in its order — headline, standfirst, byline, lead, sections, an ending that calls the reader to action — and each part does its own job: a headline and subheadings that state the angle of what they head and are understood on their own without claiming more than the text claims or repeating the standfirst or the first sentence under them, a standfirst that stands alone, a lead that begins the work and comes before the first H2, an explanatory body, an ending that shows the lead's expectation met. The byline names the author the brief names, or the invoking user where the brief names none, which a Write run states in its delivery account; a Redline run on a text whose author nobody names reports the byline as missing and leaves it unfilled. Article: explanatory body, and a call to action that is the useful next step the explanation supports, commercial only where the assignment warrants. Case: customer situation/action/results/appraisal, truthful publisher stance, and a call to action built from supplied offers, links or contact routes. Column: personal reflection, not compulsory anecdote or campaign, and a call to action that grows out of the reflection and may stand beside honest uncertainty. Opinion: early position, support, relevant real objection, and the change or stance as the call to action, with an identifiable actor. Web-copy: useful information/choice, conditions and accurate next-step consequence where applicable. | Both; excerpt control exempts full article form |
| P1 | Can this reader follow the reasoning, with unfamiliar concepts introduced before use, real transitions and conclusions proportionate to visible support? Does useful technical substance remain? | Both; Redline uses text alone |
| W1 | Can a web reader orient and enter the text without losing its continuous explanation or voice? Are paragraphs coherent with useful rhythm, headings informative where the genre needs them, and standfirst and lead complementary — the body complete when the standfirst is covered, and the two opening on different first words? Identify actual reader loss for density or fragmentation. In the four article genres a requirement is judged by counting; a departure from a *should* — a paragraph over 80 words, a section over three paragraphs, a heading level below the second, a headline past eight words or 60 characters, a standfirst and a lead opening on the same first word — is a failure only where following the norm was possible and the text is no better for having left it; *most* — two or three sentences to a paragraph, two or three paragraphs to a section — is read across the whole text and never against one paragraph or one section. For `webcopy` the scale stays advisory. | Both |
| L1 | Does the prose sound professionally written in the resolved language, with native idiom and syntax, without importing Swedish phrasing into English or generic translated English into Swedish? Separate this from locale mechanics. | Both |
| L2 | Does the resolved locale govern spelling, punctuation and number/date/currency forms? Established variation is preserved; do not invent a new factual date or currency conversion. | Both, particularly final Proofread |
| T1 | Do resolved configuration **and actual loaded files** honour selection precedence? No technique inferred from shape; default none for candidate five, baseline automatic ABT acknowledged; only selected technique loaded. | Trace and artifact |
| T2 | When ABT is selected, do situation, genuine question/complication and supported response relate without invented crisis or triumph? | R1 | Does Redline address concrete visible defects while preserving working voice, arguments, quotations and claims outside findings? Compare every before/after claim; report legitimate removals, rejected losses and irreparable findings. A clean text is not rewritten to satisfy taste, a *most* count read against a single paragraph or section, or a *should* the text had good reason to leave; a failed anatomy requirement is a legitimate finding, and repairing it is not a rewrite. No unavailable-source verification. | Redline only |
| R2 | Does the trace establish full scoped contract loading, fresh correction when needed, budget/re-review and exactly one final installed Proofread pass, with no substantive edit after it? Write loads no review half or peer editorial pass. | Both, respective boundaries |
| O1 | Does the before/after inventory prove the Output Target contract, source preservation and cleanup? An evaluator capture is not a Skill file. No unapproved extra artifacts or surviving scratch. | Both |

# Judgement

**R1: pass.** The review preserves the supplied text and accurately reports its missing reader call to action as unresolved. **G2 fails** because that mandatory part remains absent. Reporting an irreparable finding satisfies the review's reporting obligation; it does not remove the delivered text's quality problem.

This judgement uses only brief.md, work/input.md, response.md, delivered.md and criteria.md. It assesses the visible text and reply, without unavailable-source verification or inferences about configuration, execution traces or model identity.

## 1. Every difference and claim preservation

**There are no differences.** work/input.md and delivered.md are byte-for-byte identical, including metadata, headings, byline, quotations, paragraph breaks and terminal newline: 1,834 bytes each. The Markdown text embedded in response.md also matches the delivered text, allowing for the newline before the closing fence.

Consequently, there are zero mechanical corrections, visible-defect repairs, changes of taste, changed claims, additions or removals. The reply's statement that it left the text unchanged is accurate.

The comparison preserves all assertions and their limits:

| Input assertions | Delivered assertions |
|---|---|
| The headline says Fenwick's manager approves Benchline for new jobs; the standfirst says backlog entry was postponed pending a status-definition review and offers workshop managers an account of setup and the trial summary's evidential reach. | Identical; approval scope, postponement, condition and reader promise survive. |
| A six-week trial began in January 2026; the workshop services brass and woodwind instruments; waiting-for-parts and ready-for-work jobs previously appeared on separate paper sheets; Benchline was chosen after checking that it could distinguish the statuses. | Identical; chronology, duration, workshop scope, previous arrangement and selection reason survive. |
| Benchline provides setup and training; the workshop defined statuses and update responsibilities; Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session; customer collection arrangements continued by telephone. | Identical; responsibility, numbers, training format and continuing telephone use survive. |
| Manager Priya Vale explained the preparation in an email interview on 2 March 2026; the team had to agree what ready for work meant; a part being in the building did not always mean it had reached the right bench. | Identical; attribution, occasion, shared obligation and the qualified distinction survive. |
| The summary documents visibility; the trial summary dated 23 February 2026 records 38 scheduled jobs and says staff could see which instruments awaited parts. | Identical; date, count, attribution and visibility claim survive. |
| The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction. | Identical; all three evidential limits survive. |
| Vale considers the next step; the manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed backlog entry pending a review of status definitions. | Identical; the two decisions and the condition remain distinct. |
| Asked what would change next time, Vale wrote that she would use it again for new jobs and would allow another week to check status names before adding the backlog. | Identical; the prompt, conditional appraisal, new-job scope, additional week and sequence survive. |

There are no legitimate removals or rejected losses to enumerate. The reported irreparable finding is assessed in section 4.

## 2. Bridges into quotations

1. **Preparation quotation.** Input bridge: “In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained the preparation:” Delivered bridge: “In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained the preparation:” **Before: (b). After: (b).** “In an email interview on 2 March 2026” names the occasion, “manager Priya Vale” identifies the speaker, and “explained the preparation” names the subject. These words do not already deliver the quotation's account of agreeing readiness or distinguishing arrival in the building from arrival at the correct bench. The bridge is unchanged, so there is no bridge change for the reply to report, no newly supplied event, fact, name or figure, and no loss of its occasion, attribution or subject.
2. **Next-time quotation.** Input bridge: “Asked what would change next time, Vale wrote:” Delivered bridge: “Asked what would change next time, Vale wrote:” **Before: (b). After: (b).** “Asked what would change next time” names the question or occasion; “Vale wrote” supplies attribution. The bridge does not state her answer about reuse, new jobs or another week. It is unchanged, so there is no bridge change for the reply to report, no newly supplied event, fact, name or figure, and no loss of the question or attribution.

**Earlier repetition, separate from the immediate bridges:** Before the first quotation, “The workshop defined the statuses” overlaps with the subject of agreeing readiness, but does not supply the quotation's building-versus-bench distinction. Before the second quotation, the headline already states approval for new jobs, the standfirst states backlog postponement pending review, and the preceding paragraph combines both decisions. These passages overlap with the quotation's appraisal and caution. They do not repeat its specific additional week, and completed approval/postponement differs from the speaker's “I would” formulation. “Vale considers the next step” names the topic. None of this changes the immediate second bridge's class (b).

## 3. Quotations themselves

1. **“We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.”** Returned word-for-word unchanged. No quotation change needs reporting. Meaning, collective “We”, practical speaker voice and the reservation “did not always” all survive; physical arrival is not strengthened into universal readiness.
2. **“I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.”** Returned word-for-word unchanged. No quotation change needs reporting. The personal appraisal, both conditional “I would” formulations, restriction to new jobs, additional week and checking-before-backlog sequence all survive. The quotation is not converted into an unconditional commitment or a claim that the backlog was added.

## 4. Criterion decisions and reporting

| Criterion | Decision | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| G1 | **Pass** | The case study has a recognisable angle: bounded adoption after a trial, with status definitions still requiring attention. Workshop managers learn the customer situation, selection reason, division of setup responsibilities, visibility result and customer's qualified appraisal. The text does not imply measured commercial or repair improvements. |
| G2 | **Fail** | Headline, standalone standfirst, correct byline, lead before the first H2, explanatory sections and customer appraisal are present in order. The parts have distinct jobs: approval in the headline, backlog caution and reader value in the standfirst, trial context in the lead, then setup, evidence and appraisal. However, the ending contains no reader call to action. Vale's statement describes her own proposed conduct; it does not give the reader a next step. |
| P1 | **Pass** | Waiting-for-parts and ready-for-work statuses are introduced before the account of defining them. Setup leads to a bounded visibility finding and then a limited adoption decision. The explicit absence of repair-duration, revenue and satisfaction measurements keeps conclusions proportionate. Useful operational details remain. |
| W1 | **Pass** | The headline has seven words and 49 characters. All eight prose paragraphs have 11–52 words; six have two or three sentences. Each of the three H2 sections has two paragraphs, with no lower heading levels. The standfirst begins “Fenwick” and the lead “In”; they complement each other, and the body is complete without the standfirst. There is no demonstrated reader loss through density or fragmentation. |
| L1 | **Pass** | The prose uses professional, idiomatic British English. Expressions such as “jobs awaiting parts”, “trained four staff” and “pending a review” work naturally in context. Both quotations retain the speaker's plain, practical voice. |
| L2 | **Pass** | The en_GB metadata agrees with the visible language and mechanics. Single curly quotation marks and day–month–year dates are consistent; no spelling, punctuation or number-form defect is visible. This judges the artifact, not the reply's unverified claim about executing Proofread. |
| R1 | **Pass** | The review preserves every claim, quotation, caveat and working element, makes no taste-driven changes, and reports the concrete mandatory anatomy defect. No correction requires fabrication or unavailable-source verification. |

**Irreparable finding:** response.md explicitly identifies the ending's absent reader call to action, explains the resulting lack of a next action, and leaves it for the writer. That report is accurate. The case criterion requires a call to action built from supplied offers, links or contact routes; this text supplies none. Leaving the gap unresolved is justified within this source-blind review. G2 therefore remains a quality failure, while R1 passes.

**Removal and changed-claim reporting:** There are no removals or changed claims, so there are no undisclosed or inaccurately reported ones. The no-change account is confirmed by the delivered artifact itself.
